fatal_errors: The starting material is misidentified as a Ti-doped conventional W–Cu composite rather than a directionally segregated, nominally equiatomic WTaVTi refractory high-entropy alloy.

Selective dealloying is incorrectly attributed to the lower melting character of Ti-rich regions; the reported mechanism is preferential Ti–Cu exchange driven by mixing thermodynamics, with W, Ta, and V retained.

The hypothesis claims preservation of mechanical durability and irradiation resistance in the finished composite, although composite strength was not directly established and irradiation was tested only on precursor dendrites as a ligament proxy.
No supporting prior evidence or citations are supplied despite the explicit request.
explanation: The response recovers the central concept of molten-Cu liquid-metal dealloying, sacrificial Ti-rich channels, and aligned continuous Cu pathways, so it is recognizably related to the target. However, it reconstructs the precursor incorrectly and omits the WTaVTi composition, directional dendrite–interdendrite architecture, 1200 °C/96 h treatment, bicontinuous phase fractions, and approximately 300 nm W-rich passivating interlayer. Its mechanism lacks the key heats-of-mixing argument and interfacial passivation. The predicted comparison against a conventional powder-metallurgy W–Cu composite is not the principal demonstrated comparison, which was against the unprocessed WTaVTi precursor; superiority over conventional W–Cu at very high temperature was only extrapolated. It also fails to distinguish direct composite thermal measurements from proxy irradiation results and anticipated, rather than measured, mechanical durability. The proposed controlled experiment is broadly capable of testing the stated engineering claim, but it needs specified temperature ranges, dealloying parameters, matched architecture/composition, quantified mechanical criteria, and a defined irradiation species, energy, fluence, and failure threshold.
